title: Pollo alla milanese
subtitle: Breaded and fried chicken cutlet in the Milanese style
excerpt: Pollo alla milanese is a boneless chicken breast beaten thin, breaded in egg and fine breadcrumbs, and fried in butter and oil until golden. It is the chicken counterpart to the cotoletta and one of the most versatile plates in the Italian repertoire. Ready in under 20 minutes, it suits a weeknight or a summer dinner party.
sourceNotes: Italian home-cooking classic. Breaded chicken cutlets in the Milanese style are made across Italy and formed the basis for wiener schnitzel and its many relatives. Method drawn from Marcella Hazan, Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking (1992).

glossaryTerms.definition: Italian culinary term for 'in the Milanese style': referring to meat that has been dipped in beaten egg, coated in fine breadcrumbs, and fried in butter.

content.text: Pollo alla milanese is the chicken version of the famous Milanese breaded cutlet: breast meat beaten flat, crumbed, and fried until the coating is deeply golden. Cooking
requires fine, dry breadcrumbs (panko is too coarse for this), foaming butter, and speed. The cutlet should be on the plate within 8 minutes of entering the pan.

items.prepNote: halved horizontally and beaten flat to 5 mm

content.text: Beat {{chicken-breast}} of chicken breast halves flat between baking paper. Set up three wide dishes: {{plain-flour}} of seasoned flour, {{eggs}} of beaten egg, {{breadcrumbs-dried}} of fine dried breadcrumbs. Flour each piece, dip in egg, press firmly into breadcrumbs on both sides.

Heat {{unsalted-butter}} of butter and {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. When the butter foams, add the cutlets. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes per side until deeply golden. Work in batches. Season immediately with salt. Serve with lemon wedges.

items.cause: Butter not hot enough when cutlets went in.
items.fix: The butter must be foaming before the first cutlet goes in. Don't crowd the pan: each cutlet needs direct contact with the hot fat.

items.cause: Too much egg, or breadcrumbs not pressed firmly enough.
items.fix: Let the excess egg drip off. Press the crumbs on with the heel of your hand from both sides.

content.text: The Milanese cutlet has spread widely: the technique became the Wiener Schnitzel in Austria and the milanesa across South America. At home in Milan, pollo alla milanese is a quick family dinner with a green salad and lemon. It is one of the most reliable recipes in the Italian kitchen.
